title: Admin telemetry capture & compliance playbook — Hightower Capital sync
next_steps: Jordan to share SOC2/ISO artifacts and evidence packing list
Maya to provision demo tenant with audit streaming to customer S3 in us-west-2
Customer to confirm legal retention window and sensitive-data scrub rules
action_items: Jordan Kim — Send SOC 2 type II report PDF + audit log schema doc — due 2026-02-20
Maya Patel — Stand up ephemeral demo tenant with audit export to S3 + example object keys — due 2026-02-23

summary: Customer wanted a deep review of what admin and operational telemetry Redwood captures, how it can be exported (streaming vs batch), encryption/KMS model, RBAC/SSO behaviors, and options for retention and regionally resident exports for legal. Agreed next steps to stand up a demo tenant with audit streaming to customer S3 and to share SOC2 artifacts.
topics: private vs dedicated deployment audit differences
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna do a sort of focused run-through on admin telemetry and how you can get evidence out for compliance. i'm Jordan, AE, and Maya from the SE team will run the demo bits. quick roll call?
[00:18] Rajiv Menon: Rajiv here. Laura, Evan, Simone and Tom are on from Hightower. thanks — we're keen to understand what you capture and how we can get it into our systems.
[00:32] Maya Patel: Great, thanks Rajiv. I wanted to set context: we typically show three layers — UI/audit events (admin console actions), control plane events (rollouts, model pinning), and runtime operational telemetry (latency, errors). For compliance most folks focus on the first two plus admin API calls.
[01:05] Laura Chen: when you say "admin api calls" are we talking about who clicked what, role changes, token issuance, or also things like model access logs and prompt snippets?
[01:20] Maya Patel: Good question. We capture: user changes (create/update/delete user), role changes, API key lifecycle (create/revoke/rotate), SSO linkages (SAML assertions — note, not the raw assertion), policy changes (RBAC rules), model pin/rollout events, and model versioning actions. For model access we capture metadata — model id, request id, timestamp, and token usage — but we do not log full prompt text by default in audit exports unless you opt into request-body capture for debugging.
[01:58] Evan Brooks: That last bit is important. our legal team is strict about full-text retention. can you toggle that per-tenant? per-route?
[02:10] Maya Patel: Yes, we have a per-tenant flag in the private/dedicated offering and a per-route option in the hosted API that controls whether request/response bodies are included in audit export. It's off by default for privacy. Turning it on will increase storage and change the compliance posture.
[02:36] Laura Chen: And is the exported data redacted or pseudonymized?
[02:43] Diego Alvarez (CSM): We offer a couple of patterns: simple redaction rules (regex-based) at export time, and a pre-export processor for dedicated/private where you can run a lambda to scrub or tokenise fields. We'll share the pattern docs.
[03:03] Rajiv Menon: how do you deliver the logs? we want them in our SIEM with minimal glue work.
[03:12] Maya Patel: Two main patterns: streaming and batch. Streaming — we push events to a Kinesis/ PubSub-like stream or deliver over a secure syslog/HTTP webhook to your collector. Batch — periodic S3 objects in NDJSON that contain time-sliced events (per hour/day) with manifest files. Both are signed and encrypted in transit.
[03:41] Tom Ivers: For S3 export, do you support server-side encryption with our KMS? we need customer-managed keys.
[03:49] Jordan Kim: Yes — two options. For hosted customers we manage encryption keys (our KMS) but can enable envelope encryption with customer KMS in dedicated/private. For S3 export we can support SSE-KMS with customer-managed keys and BYOK integrations (HSM-backed) under Private. We'll detail key policies and rotation.
[04:12] Simone Park (Legal): Is there an audit trail of who accessed the exported artifacts inside Redwood? like did someone in support download a retention snapshot?
[04:22] Diego Alvarez: Support access is gated. We have an access review policy and every support session requires customer approval for ad-hoc exports. All internal access to customer audit artifacts is itself captured in an internal audit log we can provide in evidence packs.
[04:41] Laura Chen: you mentioned manifest files. what about verification? we need integrity verification to prove no tampering.
[04:50] Maya Patel: Each batch export object is accompanied by a signed manifest (SHA256 + signature). We can also generate a proof-of-append log window, which some customers ingest into their WORM storage.
[05:06] Rajiv Menon: residency. we need logs to stay in eu-west for EU-resident accounts and some teams in london. what do you support?
[05:16] Maya Patel: We can pin exports to a region. Hosted customers choose the region for object storage; for Dedicated and Private you control the region via your VPC/subnets. For cross-border legal holds, we support sending exports to a customer-owned bucket in target regions.
[05:36] Evan Brooks: Ok, SIEM connectors — Splunk and Datadog are essential. is schema stable? we don't want parsers constantly breaking.
[05:45] Maya Patel: The exported schema uses a stable envelope: event_type, ts, actor_id, actor_role, resource, action, request_id, meta (as a JSON string for extensible fields). We maintain semantic versioning for schema changes and publish a changelog + a compatibility mode for one major version.
[06:12] Laura Chen: what's the retention model? can we request legal hold and pull historic snapshots?
[06:20] Jordan Kim: Retention is configured per-tenant. Common presets: 7 days (default ephemeral), 90 days (standard), 365 days (extended). For legal hold we can freeze exports and provide point-in-time snapshots. There's also archive-to-glacier patterns for long term retention.
[06:38] Simone Park: If we apply legal hold, is that reversible? our legal ops wants write-once guarantees.
[06:45] Diego Alvarez: We can generate WORM-compliant objects in your S3 bucket (object lock governance mode) and provide checksums. Reversing a legal hold requires explicit contract/ops steps.
[06:58] Rajiv Menon: On RBAC — how granular are the roles? can we map SAML groups to roles?
[07:05] Maya Patel: You can map SAML groups to Redwood roles. We support a role hierarchy: owner/admin/auditor/readonly/ops. Each action is tied to a permission set; role changes are logged. We also emit impersonation events when a Redwood engineer is acting on behalf of a customer (and that is heavily flagged in the logs).
[07:33] Evan Brooks: Impersonation events are key. we need a tamper-evident record when someone from Redwood executes a remediation.
[07:40] Jordan Kim: Agreed. Those events include session id, request id, reason code, and are surfaced in the exported events.
[07:49] Laura Chen: Ok, KMS — you said envelope encryption for dedicated/private. how about key rotation and deletion policies?
[07:57] Maya Patel: We support automated rotation and a key lifecycle policy. For customer-managed keys we recommend 90-day rotation and we provide a rotation handler that re-encrypts export objects. Deletion of keys is a destructive action; we require a multi-party approval and will not rotate off keys without notice in production.
[08:18] Simone Park: Is there a way to attest to key management controls for compliance reviewers?
[08:23] Jordan Kim: Yes, our SOC2 report includes KMS control descriptions. For dedicated/private we provide architecture diagrams and your security team can run an on-site or remote KMS control review during onboarding.
[08:35] Rajiv Menon: about the event vocabulary, can you give an example event for an admin role change?
[08:42] Maya Patel: Sure. Example NDJSON line: {"event_type":"role_change","ts":"2026-02-18T15:01:12Z","actor_id":"laura.chen@hightower","actor_role":"security_admin","target_user":"tom.ivers","action":"grant_role","role":"auditor","request_id":"r-abc123","details":"via SAML group mapping"}. Note — transcription sometimes munges braces, sorry.
[09:15] Laura Chen: does that include IP address and device context?
[09:21] Maya Patel: We include source_ip, user_agent, and geo (if resolvable). For privacy-sensitive deployments geo can be omitted.
[09:33] Evan Brooks: Do you capture admin console clicks via UI? like if someone toggles a feature flag we need a proof.
[09:41] Maya Patel: UI interactions produce the same event stream with an action of "toggle_feature" and a diff in the details payload. We try to consolidate noisy UI telemetry and only persist the final state change for the audit-export.
[10:00] Rajiv Menon: about forensic readiness — in a breach scenario can we ask for a high-fidelity dump? what's your SLA?
[10:10] Diego Alvarez: For customers under active contracts (enterprise/dedicated) we have an incident support path: we can produce high-fidelity captures and extend retention windows temporarily. SLA depends on contract but typical TAT is 24 hours for evidence packaging.
[10:27] Rajiv Menon: and chain of custody?
[10:30] Diego Alvarez: We include signed manifests, access logs for who exported what, and MD5/SHA checksums. We can provide a simple chain-of-custody document for legal.
[10:42] Simone Park: GDPR question — if a EU subject asks for deletion of their data, are prompts stored in a way we can delete them?
[10:52] Maya Patel: Prompts and responses are stored per-tenant; if you enable request-body capture we store them in encrypted stores with metadata that ties to request ids and subject ids when available. We support subject deletion workflows that can purge request-bodies across storage layers, but audit manifests (which prove historical retention) are immutable; you'll need to coordinate the exact deletion semantics with your legal team.
[11:20] Laura Chen: What's the default retention on internal logs that mention customer data?
[11:25] Jordan Kim: Internally we keep service logs for 30 days and aggregated metrics longer. Sensitive debug logs (that might contain PII) are time-limited and only kept for 7 days unless a retention extension is requested.
[11:40] Evan Brooks: How do we test the export pipeline? is there a replay mode?
[11:45] Maya Patel: We provide a sandbox replay utility that can stream a 7-day window of anonymized events to your SIEM for parser validation. We'll run it during the demo tenant provisioning.
[11:58] Rajiv Menon: Are there compliance packs for auditors?
[12:03] Jordan Kim: Yes: SOC2 Type II report, ISO 27001 statement of applicability, encryption key diagrams, and sample audit exports. We'll attach a vendor evidence pack.
[12:15] Laura Chen: When we do the demo tenant, can you enable an option to include request bodies but redact PII automatically? we have a compliance engineering team that prefers redaction over full blackboxing.
[12:27] Maya Patel: Yep. For dedicated/private we can run pre-export processors that apply redaction regex sets and tokenization. For hosted we have managed redaction rules but they'll be less customizable.
[12:44] Evan Brooks: About logs for model outputs — do you capture completions that might contain PII in embeddings or LLM output?
[12:52] Maya Patel: We capture model metadata by default. If you opt-in to capture outputs, those will be treated as request-bodies. We also offer an embeddings-only flag where raw vectors are stored without decoding.
[13:10] Rajiv Menon: One more question: how do you handle service account actions? we often have automated jobs that rotate models.
[13:18] Maya Patel: Service accounts are tied to machine principals; their actor_id is the service name. Actions by service accounts are logged and can be mapped back to CI/CD pipelines. We also support key-scoped permissions to narrow what those accounts can do.
[13:34] Simone Park: On legal hold and eDiscovery, can you export in formats courts accept?
[13:40] Diego Alvarez: We can produce NDJSON, CSV, and PDF evidence packs with signed manifests and chain-of-custody notes. We'll work with your legal ops on formatting.
[13:55] Laura Chen: any thoughts on threat detection — can you stream to our detection pipeline in near real-time?
[14:02] Maya Patel: Yes, streaming will push events in ~1-2s latency to your collector; you can run correlation rules on actor behaviors and alert on policy violations.
[14:14] Evan Brooks: If something is flagged, can we trigger off automated remediation from our side?
[14:19] Maya Patel: You can trigger via our webhooks or the API to enact remedial actions; those remediation calls are themselves logged and exported so you get an audit trail.
[14:33] Rajiv Menon: risk question — if we use your hosted offering, is there any chance Redwood engineers can read our request bodies?
[14:42] Jordan Kim: By default, no. Request bodies are encrypted at rest and access is restricted. For debugging we require explicit customer approval and those sessions are logged and time-bound. We also recommend dedicated if you want stricter isolation.
[14:58] Laura Chen: Can you give a quick walkthrough of the demo tenant configuration you'll provision?
[15:05] Maya Patel: Sure. We'll create a tenant in us-west-2, enable S3 batch exports to a customer-owned bucket in that region, enable streaming webhooks to your dev Splunk endpoint, turn on role-change audit events, and provide a short replay dataset. We'll also enable an opt-in request-body capture for a limited test path and a redaction processor.
[15:33] Rajiv Menon: timeline?
[15:35] Jordan Kim: We said earlier — Maya will stand up the tenant by EOD Monday (2026-02-23), Jordan will send SOC2 artifacts by Friday (2026-02-20), Laura to confirm retention window by Wednesday (2026-02-24).
[15:52] Simone Park: One more governance Q — who signs off on key policies?
[15:57] Diego Alvarez: Typically the customer's security lead plus the assigned Redwood AE sign off the KMS integration runbook. We'll schedule a short security onboarding with your team.
[16:08] Laura Chen: thanks — that sounds good.
[16:12] Jordan Kim: quick recap then: we'll share the evidence pack and schema, provision a demo tenant with exports to your S3 + Splunk, provide replay, and document redaction options. any blockers?
[16:25] Rajiv Menon: no blockers, we just want to validate parser stability and legal hold behavior.
[16:31] Evan Brooks: also want to test impersonation logging in the replay.
[16:35] Maya Patel: we'll include impersonation events and a demo of the support-access workflow.
[16:40] Tom Ivers: log format question — if we want more fields, like kubernetes pod ids, can we extend the meta?
[16:47] Maya Patel: meta is extensible; for dedicated/private we can add extra keys from your runtime env. For hosted it's more limited but we can add common ones.
[16:58] Simone Park: ok thanks all. we'll expect the docs and the tenant details.
[17:03] Jordan Kim: great — thanks for the time. we'll send follow-ups and set up the security onboarding meeting.
[17:10] [Call ends — 00:58:02 recorded]

Notes: transcript has occasional mis-hearings and filler words; some technical terms may be slightly off in transcription (e.g., K-V cache transcribed as K-V cash). Refer to attached artifacts for canonical schemas and manifests.
